<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let $q=p^{s}\ge3$, $n\ge1$, $N=q^{n}$ and $P=P_{q,n}$ as in \eqref{eq:family}. Put
$R=(N-1)/(q-1)=1+q+\dots+q^{n-1}$ and $k=1+(q-2)R$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\deg P=(q-2)N$ and $k=(\deg P+1)/(q-1)$, an exact division;
\item[(ii)] $L(\mathfrak{C}_{P},t,T)$ does not depend on $t$, lies in $\mathbb{F}_p[T]$, and
\[
   L(\mathfrak{C}_{P},T)\ =\ \prod_{\nu\in E^{n}/(\mathbb{Z}/n)}
      \Bigl(1-\operatorname{wt}(\nu)\,T^{\operatorname{per}(\nu)}\Bigr);
\]
\item[(iii)] $\deg_T L(\mathfrak{C}_P,T)=|E|^{n}$;
\item[(iv)] $\displaystyle r(\mathfrak{C}_{P})\ =\ \sum_{\substack{\nu\in E^{n}/(\mathbb{Z}/n)\\ \operatorname{wt}(\nu)=1}}
   p^{\,v_p(\operatorname{per}(\nu))}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:ppower}
If $n$ is a power of $p$ then
\[
   r\bigl(\mathfrak{C}_{P_{q,n}}\bigr)\ =\ \Bigl(\frac{q}{p}\Bigr)^{\!n}(p-1)^{\,n-1}
   \ =\ \frac{|E|^{n}}{p-1}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:unbounded}
For every $q\ge3$ the analytic ranks of the twists of the Carlitz module over $\mathbb{F}_q$ are
unbounded. Problem 1.4 of \cite{GL25} therefore has a negative answer for every $q$, and
its parts (a) and (b), which were conditional on a positive answer, do not arise.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:GL}
$L(\mathfrak{C}_P,t,T)=\det\bigl(I_k-\mathfrak{M}(P,1,k)T\bigr)$ for every $k\ge (m+1)/(q-1)$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:k}
With $m=\deg P_{q,n}=(q-2)N$ one has $(m+1)/(q-1)=1+(q-2)R=k$, an integer, and
$k-1=(q-2)R<N$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
$m+1=(q-2)N+1=(q-2)(N-1)+(q-1)=(q-2)(q-1)R+(q-1)=(q-1)\bigl[(q-2)R+1\bigr]$.
For the inequality, $k-1=(q-2)(N-1)/(q-1)<N-1<N$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:coeff}
Write $s_l=(N-1)l+(q-2)$ for $0\le l\le q-2$. The exponents $s_l$ are pairwise distinct,
$P_{q,n}=\sum_{l=0}^{q-2}c_l\,\theta^{s_l}$ with
$c_l=(-1)^{q-l}\binom{q-2}{l}$, and in $\mathbb{F}_p$
\[
   c_l\ =\ (-1)^{q}\,(l+1).
\]
In particular $c_l\neq0$ if and only if $l\in E$, and all coefficients of $P_{q,n}$ lie in
the prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
$\theta^{N}-\theta=\theta(\theta^{N-1}-1)$, so
$P_{q,n}=\theta^{q-2}(\theta^{N-1}-1)^{q-2}
 =\sum_{l=0}^{q-2}\binom{q-2}{l}(-1)^{q-2-l}\theta^{(N-1)l+q-2}$,
and $(-1)^{q-2-l}=(-1)^{q-l}$. The exponents are distinct because $N-1>q-2$. Finally, in
$\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]$,
\[
   (1+x)^{p^{s}-2}=\frac{1+x^{p^{s}}}{(1+x)^{2}}
   \equiv\sum_{l\ge0}(-1)^{l}(l+1)x^{l} \pmod{x^{p^{s}}},
\]
whence $\binom{q-2}{l}\equiv(-1)^{l}(l+1)$ for $0\le l\le q-2$, and
$c_l=(-1)^{q-l}(-1)^{l}(l+1)=(-1)^{q}(l+1)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:notboth}
No entry of $\mathfrak{M}$ has both a nonzero coefficient of $t$ and a nonzero constant term.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
This would force $(N-1)(l-l')=1$ for some $l,l'\in E$, impossible since $N-1\ge2$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:unique}
Let $x\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$ and $l\in E$. If $l>x_{n-1}$ then $qx-(N-1)l\le-2$, and if
$l<x_{n-1}$ then $qx-(N-1)l\ge N>k-1$. If $l=x_{n-1}$ then $qx-(N-1)l=\sigma(x)$.
Consequently $x$ has at most one outgoing $t$-edge and at most one outgoing flat edge
inside $\{0,\dots,k-1\}$; both require $l=x_{n-1}\in E$, the flat one landing on
$\sigma(x)$ and the $t$-edge on $\sigma(x)+1$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Writing $qx=x_{n-1}N+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}x_{i-1}q^{i}$ and $(N-1)l=lN-l$ gives
\[
   qx-(N-1)l=(x_{n-1}-l)N+\Delta+l,
   \qquad \Delta:=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}x_{i-1}q^{i}\in[0,\,N-q].
\]
If $l\ge x_{n-1}+1$ then the value is at most $-N+(N-q)+(q-2)=-2$. If
$l\le x_{n-1}-1$ then it is at least $N$, and $N>k-1$ by Lemma \ref{lem:k}. If
$l=x_{n-1}$ the value is $\Delta+x_{n-1}=\sigma(x)$. The statement for $t$-edges follows
by adding $1$, which changes $-2$ into $-1$ and $N$ into $N+1$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:disjoint}
The circuits of the flat-edge digraph are pairwise vertex-disjoint.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:nofront}
No circuit of the digraph of $\mathfrak{M}$ uses a $t$-edge.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:unique} an edge leaves a vertex $z$ only if $l=z_{n-1}\in E$, so in
particular $z_{n-1}\le q-2$. A flat edge sends $z$ to $\sigma(z)$, which has the same
multiset of digits, hence the same digit sum. A $t$-edge sends $z$ to $\sigma(z)+1$; the
digit of $\sigma(z)$ in position $0$ is $z_{n-1}\le q-2$, so adding $1$ produces the digit
$z_{n-1}+1\le q-1$ with no carry, and $\Sigma$ increases by exactly $1$. Thus $\Sigma$ is
nondecreasing along any walk and strictly increases at every $t$-edge. A circuit returns to
its origin, so it contains no $t$-edge.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:necklace}
The circuits of the digraph of $\mathfrak{M}$ are exactly the orbits of $E^{n}$ under $\sigma$. A
circuit has length $\operatorname{per}(\nu)$, which divides $n$, and weight $\operatorname{wt}(\nu)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:nofront} a circuit uses flat edges only, and by Lemma \ref{lem:unique}
the map along it is $\sigma$. Since $\sigma^{n}=\mathrm{id}$ on $n$-digit strings, its
length divides $n$; and every digit of a vertex on the circuit occupies the leading
position at some step, so all its digits lie in $E$.

Conversely let $x\in E^{n}$. All digits of $x$ are at most $q-2$, so
$\sigma(x)\le(q-2)(1+q+\dots+q^{n-1})=(q-2)R=k-1$: the flat edge from $x$ exists and lands
in range, and $\sigma(x)\in E^{n}$. Hence the $\sigma$-orbit of $x$ is a circuit. The
weight is the product of the edge weights, which by \eqref{eq:weight} is
$\prod_{m<\operatorname{per}(\nu)}(w_m+1)=\operatorname{wt}(\nu)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The word $(q-2,q-2,\dots,q-2)$ is a fixed point of $\sigma$, so it contributes a circuit of
length $1$ and weight $q-1$. In $\mathbb{F}_p$ one has $q-1=-1$, so this circuit contributes
$1$ to $r$ when $p=2$ and $0$ otherwise. This is exactly the trivial zero of
\cite[Proposition 4.4]{GL16}: its two hypotheses are $m\equiv-1\pmod{q-1}$, which holds
because $m=(q-2)q^{n}\equiv q-2$, and $a_m=-1$, which for $P_{q,n}$ -- whose leading
coefficient is $1$ -- holds precisely in characteristic $2$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $n=p^{a}$. Every $d$ dividing $n$ is a power of $p$, so $p^{v_p(d)}=d$ and
Theorem \ref{thm:main}(iv) reads $r=\sum_{\operatorname{wt}(\nu)=1}\operatorname{per}(\nu)$. Moreover, for a word
$w\in\nu$ of period $d$ one has $\prod_{m=0}^{n-1}(w_m+1)=\operatorname{wt}(\nu)^{n/d}$ with $n/d$ a
power of $p$; since raising to a power of $p$ is injective on $\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$ (a group of
order $p-1$, prime to $p$), the condition $\operatorname{wt}(\nu)=1$ is equivalent to
$\prod_{m=0}^{n-1}(w_m+1)=1$. Hence
\[
   r=\sum_{\operatorname{wt}(\nu)=1}\operatorname{per}(\nu)
    =\#\Bigl\{\,w\in E^{n}\ :\ \textstyle\prod_{m=0}^{n-1}(w_m+1)=1\ \text{in }\mathbb{F}_p\,\Bigr\}.
\]
The map $l\mapsto l+1$ is a bijection from $E$ onto
$V=\{v\in[1,q-1]:p\nmid v\}$. Since $p\mid q$, each residue class modulo $p$ contains
exactly $q/p$ elements of $[0,q-1]$; removing $v=0$ leaves exactly $q/p$ elements of $V$ in
each nonzero class, so $|V|=(p-1)q/p=|E|$ and the reduction $V\to\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$ is
$(q/p)$-to-one. By orthogonality of the characters of $\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$,
\[
   \#\{w : \textstyle\prod(w_m+1)=1\}
   =\frac{1}{p-1}\sum_{\chi}\Bigl(\sum_{v\in V}\chi(v)\Bigr)^{\!n}
   =\frac{1}{p-1}\Bigl(\frac{q}{p}(p-1)\Bigr)^{\!n}
   =\Bigl(\frac{q}{p}\Bigr)^{\!n}(p-1)^{n-1},
\]
because $\sum_{v\in V}\chi(v)=(q/p)\sum_{r\in\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}}\chi(r)$ vanishes for
$\chi\neq1$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Since $q\ge3$ we have $|E|=q-q/p\ge2$, so
$(q/p)^{n}(p-1)^{n-1}=|E|^{n}/(p-1)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ along the powers of $p$; by
Corollary \ref{cor:ppower} the ranks $r(\mathfrak{C}_{P_{q,p^{a}}})$ are unbounded.

It remains to check that these are pairwise non-isomorphic twists. If $P_1,P_2$ are free
from $(q-1)$-st powers and $P_1/P_2=f^{\,q-1}$ with $f\in\mathbb{F}_q(\theta)^{*}$, write
$f=g/h$ in lowest terms; then $P_1h^{q-1}=P_2g^{q-1}$, so for every irreducible $\pi$ one
has $v_{\pi}(P_1)\equiv v_{\pi}(P_2)\pmod{q-1}$, and since both valuations lie in
$[0,q-2]$ they are equal. Thus $P_1$ and $P_2$ have the same irreducible factors with the
same multiplicities. Now the irreducible factors of $P_{q,n}$ are exactly the monic
irreducibles of degree dividing $n$, the largest such degree being $n$; hence $P_{q,n}$ and
$P_{q,n'}$ define the same twist only if $n=n'$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
